Summary: The paper presents a controlled benchmark for writing knowledge-base entries from exactly the papers the curators cited. It uses 100 OMIM phenotype entries with 2-12 references each (515 papers, 19% readable in full through open access; causal gene withheld). One model (Claude Opus 5.5) drafts every entry under six strategies: direct reading, an agentic curator, an evidence graph, case table first, recall-then-verify, and a memory-only control. Three add-ons are also tested: second-hand passages from citing papers, a reconciled case database, and a learned curation guide. All strategies share the same guards, one claim-level audit with one repair round, and one scoring. The primary endpoint is coverage of fact lists split once, before any draft, from OMIM allelic-variant descriptions deposited in ClinVar (6,652 facts over 476 paragraphs). The main results are these. Hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries; +43.7 points, 95% CI +38.3 to +49.1; 45 better, 0 worse, 1 tied; Sec. 4.1, Table 24). Direct reading, the agentic curator and the evidence graph lie within 0.7 points of one another on the 93 compared entries, and convey 93.6-94.4% of the facts the supplied text is judged to state (Tables 1-2). The case-table-first implementation trails by 1.9 points, most of it on full-text papers. The memory-based strategies convey about 15%. Released PaperQA2 and GraphRAG pipelines convey fewer facts at higher cost, on 10 and 4 entries; STORM could not run because the model's safety filter stopped its prompts. Planted errors show that the audit catches swapped citations and moved sentences, but not over-citation, omissions or most broadened claims. All three reviewers rate the paper 5 (Reject) with confidence 4. They agree that the design is clean, the statistics careful and the reporting unusually candid, and that the within-paper access manipulation is a genuine causal result. The main claims are nonetheless not yet sufficiently supported for the main track, for three reasons. No judgement in the measurement chain is validated by a person. Only one model family writes, audits and judges. The headline strategy comparison is a near-null, obtained in a regime chosen so that direct reading should do well, while the regimes where strategies could differ were not completed. The released-system comparison is too small and too modified to support its place in the abstract. Decision: Reject. A human-validated sample of the judgements, together with a judge (and ideally a writer) from a second model family, would address the shared core concern. Equivalence-style statistics and a more measured abstract would address most of the remaining points.
Strengths: Clean experimental control (all reviewers). The model, cited papers, guards, audit and scoring are the same for every strategy, and the fact lists are fixed once without sight of any draft, so denominators are identical across strategies (Sec. 3.3). Table 7 shows why this matters: splitting facts afresh for each draft gives levels 2-5 points higher.

The within-paper access manipulation is a genuine causal test with a large, consistent effect. It uses the same 46 entries and 2,120 fixed facts with full text hidden or available: +43.7 points (+38.3 to +49.1), higher with full text in 45 entries and tied in 1 (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2, Table 24). This far exceeds the measured judge variation (95.7% per-fact agreement, Table 21) and replicate noise (+/-1.0 point, App. E). Attribution analyses make the result concrete. Of missed facts, 49% were stated in the available text for full-text papers versus 2% for abstract-only papers (Fig. 3, Table 18). Only 24 (1.7%) of 1,420 facts fully conveyed from abstract-only papers are stated in no supplied text (Table 19).

Completion is treated as an outcome (all reviewers). Strategies are compared under a symmetric inclusion rule, with an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Tables 6, 12). The paper also discloses that an earlier asymmetric rule produced a spurious 2.1-point gap, larger than the true differences between reading strategies, and a frameshift-naming bug (App. I.4). This is a transferable lesson for LLM-pipeline evaluation, where refusals and stopped replies are common.

The statistical reporting is careful and checkable. It includes paired bootstrap intervals over entries, better/worse/tied counts, exact sign tests, Holm adjustment on the secondary measures, and separate judge-variation and run-to-run studies used as a yardstick rather than a test (Tables 8-9, 21; App. E). The reported sign-test p-values recompute correctly: 31/48 gives 0.071, 33/45 gives 0.213 and 31/42 gives 0.242 (Sec. 4.2); 1/9 gives 0.021 (Sec. 4.4); and with 4 entries the smallest attainable p is 0.125.

The audit stress test yields a concrete, non-obvious finding (all reviewers). Best-verdict aggregation over cited papers hides over-citation: 0 of 30 added citations were flagged, although the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' on all 176 claims attributed to it (Table 44). Omissions are invisible by construction. In the real drafts, 4-7% of claim-paper pairs in multi-citation paragraphs are not supported (Table 47). Passages from later papers can pass claims that the full text contradicts (Table 25). These are useful cautions for FActScore-style verification of cited text.

The reporting is unusually candid. It includes null or negative results for all three add-ons (Tables 26-28), the deviations from the design (App. J), a contamination analysis by creation era plus a held-out set of entries created in 2026 (Fig. 5, App. I.2), and a thorough limitations list (Sec. 5, items i-xi).

The benchmark is built only from public resources, and the curator text's rights are handled responsibly (fact identifiers, not wording). The harness and the per-entry drafts, verdicts and scores are released, and full token and cost accounting is given (Reproducibility statement; Table 13), so new strategies can be scored against the same fixed facts.
Weaknesses: No human validation anywhere in the measurement chain (all reviewers; the decisive concern). The writer's model family does the fact splitting, the present/partly/absent/contradicted marks, the 'stated in the supplied text' judgement, the audit verdicts and the completeness check (Sec. 3.3; Limitation i). The 95.7% agreement between judgings (Table 21) measures self-consistency, not validity. In Sec. 4.3 and Table 2 the same model judges both whether a fact is 'stated' and whether the draft 'conveyed' it, so errors in the two judgements may be correlated, and the 93.6-94.4% stated-fact figure may partly be an artefact. Self-preference (Panickssery et al., 2024) could also act differently on the different strategies' output styles. For a paper whose first contribution is a benchmark, this is a major gap.

A single proprietary model family writes, audits and judges (Sec. 3.2, App. B), and not even the judge is varied. The central claim, that what the strategy reads limits agreement more than how it reads, may hold only for a strong long-context model on inputs that fit one prompt. With weaker, shorter-context or open-weight models, intermediate representations or agents may matter more. Several conclusions, about released systems and about large inputs, are partly conclusions about this model's safety filter.

The tested regime favours the expected result, and the regime where strategies could differ was not completed. Entries have 2-12 references, a median of 39,450 characters (Table 38) and 81% of papers abstract- or title-only, so all papers fit one prompt. Padding added only unrelated papers, which no draft cited (Sec. 4.5, App. J.2), so it tests size, not crowding. The large-entry tier yielded no compared entry (Table 43), and the 30-75-reference tier has 10 entries with unreliable intervals (App. I.1). The authors themselves call the direction expected (Sec. 1; end of Sec. 2), so the new knowledge is mainly the effect size. Within this regime the benchmark discriminates weakly between designs: stated-fact coverage sits near a ceiling (94%; 95.5-97.1% on abstract-only papers, where most entries tie; Sec. 4.3).

The statistical framing of the strategy comparison is firmer than the evidence. 'Within about a point' (Abstract; Sec. 4.2) is asserted without an equivalence margin, TOST or minimum detectable difference. It rests on intervals that include or touch zero, e.g. the agentic curator at -0.6 (-1.3, +0.0). The paper itself shows that measurement choices move differences by about 2 points (Sec. 4.2; App. I.4), and the replicate-noise half-width is 1.0 point. The flat statement that case table first 'trails them' (Abstract) rests on -1.9 (-3.1, -0.8) with sign-test p = 0.071 (Table 9). Under intention to treat it becomes -1.4 (-4.2, +1.4) with p = 0.082 (Table 12), and the primary endpoint is not adjusted across the five comparisons with direct reading (Sec. 3.3). The more convincing evidence is the deficit on facts stated in full-text papers, -8.4 (-14.3, -3.8), 9/28/3 (Table 20), and that result should carry the claim.

Strategy is confounded with implementation. The matched ablation moves case table first by +2.1 (+1.1 to +3.2), the same size as its deficit. It changes extraction effort and synopsis-term choice together, and attributes the gain to extraction effort only by inference (Sec. 4.2; App. F). On the same 38 ablation entries, the matched evidence graph exceeds direct reading by +1.8 (+0.4 to +3.3) (Table 23), which Sec. 4.2 does not report. Paradigm-level conclusions therefore rest on single in-house implementations whose details move results by as much as the paradigm differences.

The reference is narrow and indirect. The primary endpoint uses variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs from OMIM gene entries, not the phenotype-entry narrative the drafts emulate (Sec. 3.1; Limitation ii). Only about 24% of a direct-reading draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference, and drafts make about twice as many statements per paper as the paragraph has facts (24.0 vs 11.9; App. H). Roughly three quarters of each draft is therefore checked only by the same-model audit, for fidelity rather than correctness. Strategies could differ substantially on that unscored portion (clinical description, organisation, synthesis across papers).

The endpoint is recall-type coverage with half credit for 'partly present', and it has no reference-anchored precision measure. Apart from facts contradicted (0.3-0.5%, Table 7), nothing penalises unsupported or superfluous content. Draft length differs among the reading strategies (97.3-117.9 audited claims per entry, Table 7), so verbosity is not controlled. Paired differences without partial credit are not reported, although Table 7 gives the corresponding levels.

The released-system comparison is too small and too modified to carry weight, yet it is foregrounded in the Abstract and Sec. 6. PaperQA2 ran on 10 entries and GraphRAG on 4, and with 4 entries no sign test can reach 0.05 (Sec. 4.4; Table 3). PaperQA2 ran without its agent. Every system used one small local embedder in place of its default (Tables 32-33). The systems answered six section questions rather than writing an entry, and only the strategies' drafts went through the repair round. STORM produced nothing (App. J.1). Indexing a handful of papers per entry for six queries is also the usage pattern that maximises GraphRAG's relative cost.

Attrition from the safety filter is opaque and possibly non-random. Stopped replies remove 7 of 100 main entries, 10 of 30 entries created in 2026, every large entry and every STORM run (Tables 4, 6, 30, 43), and their reasons are not visible (Sec. 3.2). If the stops correlate with disease content (e.g. lethal, reproductive or paediatric phenotypes), the compared set is a biased subsample, yet there is no analysis of which entries or papers were stopped. Together with the absence of temperature or seed control (Reproducibility statement), and the agentic curator's paper-opening behaviour being self-reported rather than logged, this makes exact reproduction impossible and ties the results to one provider at one point in time.

The padding result is summarised selectively. Sec. 4.5 and Takeaway (4) say that no strategy lost more than about a point, and they treat direct reading's rise as noise, citing only the P2 figures. Table 40 also shows the strategy-by-size interaction against direct reading at P1: -2.8 (-4.3, -1.1) for the agentic curator, -3.8 (-7.5, -0.3) for the evidence graph and -4.6 (-7.2, -1.5) for case table first. Direct reading's own P1 gain is +3.6 (+1.0, +5.9). Under the symmetric rule (Table 41, 2 entries), case table first loses 3.0 points. With 6 entries neither reading is reliable, but the main text should present both.

Reading and recall are only partly separated. Within abstract-only papers, direct-reading coverage falls from 49.8% in the 600000-609999 band to 37.9% in the newest band (Sec. 4.2; Table 16), and the memory-only control conveys 24.1% in that band (Table 17). Memory of the public OMIM and ClinVar text could also guide which stated facts a draft selects, without leaving a provenance trace. The stated-fact analysis (Table 2) is not reported by creation band or for the 2026 set, which has only 20 compared entries and five strategies (App. I.2).

The presentation is very dense, and the paper's relevance to the ICLR audience rests on modest measurement lessons. The main text packs about 15 experiments into 10 pages, with heavy hedging, rapidly introduced domain vocabulary (OMIM, ClinVar, HPO, MedGen, mim2gene) and frequent pointers to 47 appendix tables. It never shows a worked example (an entry, its fixed fact list, a draft paragraph with its audit verdicts). Side experiments on 2-10 entries, or with 2-8 items per rule (App. J, cut to about a third of their design), dilute the focus without changing the conclusions. No new method is proposed: the strategies re-implement known paradigms, and the learned guide's held-out effect is +1.0 (+0.0 to +2.0) (Table 28).
Questions: Can you add a human validation study on a stratified random sample? It should cover (a) fact splits (atomicity, faithfulness), (b) present/partly/absent/contradicted marks, (c) 'stated in the supplied text' judgements and (d) audit verdicts, report agreement with the model judge, and say whether the 0.5-2-point strategy differences lie within judge error. Even 200-300 items per type would materially strengthen Tables 1-2.

Can the existing drafts and fact lists be re-judged by a judge from a different model family, which is inexpensive relative to the study? Can at least direct reading and the evidence graph be regenerated with a second writer (ideally an open-weight long-context model) on the 93 compared entries or the 30-entry replicate subset? Do the access conclusion and the ordering of the reading strategies survive?

What paired difference in OMIM facts conveyed do you consider practically negligible? Do equivalence tests (TOST) at that margin support the 'close' claim for the agentic curator and the evidence graph? What is the minimum detectable paired difference at n = 93? Does the case-table-first deficit survive a Holm adjustment across the five comparisons with direct reading?

How sensitive are the paired differences to the half credit for 'partly present' (add paired differences on 'fully conveyed' to Table 8)? Does a length-normalised or precision-aware endpoint, or coverage per audited claim, change the ordering?

What characterises the entries and papers the safety filter stopped (disorder category, paediatric, prenatal or reproductive content, paper type)? Does the access effect or the strategy ranking change when the analysis is restricted to entries with no stopped call in any condition? Can the large entries and STORM be run through a direct API or with a second model, so that the regime in which strategies might separate becomes testable?

Would a forced context budget (e.g. capping the prompt at a fraction of the total input), or a harder subset (full-text-heavy entries, facts stated only outside the abstract), test the access-versus-strategy claim where strategy has room to matter?

Is Table 2 available by creation band and for the 2026 entries? If stated-fact coverage stays near 94% there, memory-guided selection of curator-salient facts would be largely ruled out as a driver of the 'reading strategies convey more than nine in ten stated facts' result.
How do you reconcile the negative P1 interactions and direct reading's P1 gain in Table 40 with the summary in Sec. 4.5 and Takeaway (4)?

Can the matched ablation be split into its two component changes? How should the matched evidence graph's +1.8 (+0.4 to +3.3) over direct reading (Table 23) be read against 'three reading strategies are close'?

For the released systems, how does the gap change if (a) the strategies' drafts are scored before repair (cheap, given the +0.2-point repair effect in Table 24), (b) PaperQA2 runs with its agent through a function-calling interface, (c) default or stronger embedders are used, and (d) GraphRAG runs on more entries?

The reference covers about 24% of draft statements. Has the correctness, not only the self-audited fidelity, of a sample of the remaining statements been checked, e.g. against full text, and what fraction would a curator accept for the entry?

Can the qualifier-deletion classes be scaled up? They have 2-8 items per rule (Table 45), and App. J.4 notes that only 5 of 8 hedge edits change the claim and that about 3 of 8 zygosity edits are nearly meaning-preserving. Scaling up would let the claim that the audit misses most broadened claims rest on more than a handful of genuinely broadening items.

Will the fact-list identifiers, prompts and reply cache be released, together with a versioned procedure for rebuilding the reference as ClinVar changes, so that new strategies can be scored against exactly the same denominators and judges?
Limitations: The authors' limitations section (Sec. 5, items i-xi) is thorough and candid, and the reviewers agree with all of its items. The most consequential are the absence of any human validation and the untested large-reference regime, which together limit how far the 'strategy matters little' conclusion generalises.

Not discussed enough: completion, the large-entry results and the STORM outcome depend on one provider's opaque, time-varying safety filter, and the resulting attrition may be correlated with disease content, making the compared subset non-random.

Not discussed enough: the reference text itself (OMIM descriptions in ClinVar) is public. Memory of it could guide which supplied facts a draft selects, which provenance checks cannot detect. The creation-era analysis and the 20-entry 2026 set address this only partly.

Not discussed enough: conclusions about paradigms rest on single in-house implementations whose details (e.g. extraction effort) move results by as much as the paradigm differences. In the tested regime, the benchmark's power to separate strategies is near the noise floor, which limits its use as a leaderboard.
Costs are list prices for one model, and GraphRAG's per-entry indexing over a few papers is charged in full, so the cost comparison does not carry over to other deployment patterns.
The ethics statement correctly states that generated entries are drafts for expert review, not clinical guidance, and must be marked as machine generated and not as OMIM content.
